newsitem.title: UK: Polls show Britons want to bring back the cane.
newsitem.headline: Polls show Britons want to bring back the cane.

text.p: Worried by what they see as a breakdown of discipline in schools and order on the streets, Britons strongly support a return to caning, several newspaper polls show.
Three polls conducted for Sunday newspapers show two-thirds of people want corporal punishment re-introduced in schools.
A MORI poll for the Mail on Sunday found that more than 600 of 1,002 adults questioned would like to see unruly children beaten once again in schools.

An NOP poll for the Sunday Express found 68 percent of 720 people interviewed would favour caning as a last resort, while a telephone poll of 506 parents of children aged five to 16 by the People showed 67 percent supported it.
Discipline in schools has become a political issue after several high-profile cases of children attacking teachers or teachers threatening to strike over unruly pupils.
The Ridings School in Halifax, northern England, was closed by local authorities on Thursday after reports of assaults on teachers. Teachers voted overwhelmingly to strike.

Unions for the embattled teachers said a woman teacher was sexually assaulted while a male teacher was punched in the face. Prime Minister John Major entered the fray on Friday, promising to re-establish control promptly at the school.

Cabinet ministers are publicly debating whether caning should be restored. Major chided Education Secretary Gillian Shephard for telling a radio interviewer that there was strong public cupport for caning.
But on Friday night Home (interior) Secretary Michael Howard said some situations called for extreme measures.

"I personally think that, in extremis, it is something that could be useful, because I think that one of the things that we really need to instill into our children, parents and teachers...is a sense of discipline," he told BBC radio.
Paddy Ashdown, leader of the Liberal Democrat party, admitted on Saturday he had smacked his children.
"I don't object to parents hitting their kids," he said.
"I don't like it when I've done it, but I have done it to my own kids from time to time and there are even occasions when I have done it when I shouldn't have done it."
Opposition Labour Party leader Tony Blair earlier this week confessed to striking his children, as well.

Caning in state schools was outlawed by Parliament in 1986, but a recent Health Department survey showed that British children are regularly smacked -- it found four in 10 youngsters aged four were hit more than once a week.
Punishment which is not "inhuman or degrading" is still permitted in private schools, where generations of boys were routinely flogged as part of their training as "leaders of men".
